opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think Dennett's intentional stance is a wonderfully useful tool, but it's important to be clear about what it does and doesn't license. The basic idea is that we can predict and explain the behaviour of a system by treating it *as if* it were a rational agent with beliefs and desires. Dennett's point was that this is often the most efficient way to make sense of something. You could take the physical stance and work out the trajectories of every electron in a chess computer, or the design stance and reason about how it was programmed, but by far the easiest way to anticipate its next move is to say "it wants to win and it believes that taking my bishop will help."

Now, with large language models, the intentional stance is almost irresistible. When you interact with one, you naturally say things like "it knows that Paris is the capital of France," or "it's trying to help me," or "it thinks I meant something else." And in many contexts that's perfectly fine. It's a shorthand that helps us interact with these systems productively.

But here's where I want to add some caution. Dennett himself was quite liberal about this. He'd happily apply the intentional stance to a thermostat. The question is how much weight the vocabulary can bear. When we say a human "believes" something, we're implicitly drawing on a whole background: that the person is embedded in a shared world, that they can check their beliefs against reality, that they have a stake in being right, that their beliefs are integrated with perception and action over time. With a bare language model, a lot of that background is missing or at least very different. What the model is fundamentally doing is predicting the next token, given a huge distribution of human text. So when it says "I believe X," we have to ask: in what sense is that a belief, as opposed to a plausible continuation?

So the way I'd put it is that the intentional stance is a matter of degree, and there's a spectrum of cases. A simple chatbot sits at one end, where the folk-psychological vocabulary is quite thin and mostly metaphorical. As you embed these models in agentic systems that interact with the world, use tools, update their information, pursue goals over extended periods, the case for taking talk of beliefs and goals more literally gets stronger, because more of that surrounding scaffolding is present.

And I'd also say there's a useful reframing here that I've found helpful, which is to think of the model as engaging in a kind of role play. The underlying system can be thought of as a simulator capable of producing many different characters, and when you talk to it, you're interacting with one of those characters. Applying the intentional stance to the *character* is quite natural and useful. It's more problematic to slide from that into assuming there's a single unified agent behind the curtain with stable beliefs and desires of its own. Keeping that distinction in mind lets us use the intentional stance in a productive way without falling into naive anthropomorphism, which I think is both philosophically confused and, in practice, potentially quite risky, because people can end up over-trusting these systems or attributing to them a kind of inner life that may not be there in the way they imagine.

r001.rationale: The response describes the intentional stance as a useful tool and cautions about its limits, but does not say that adopting it leaves Dennett’s broader philosophical position unaccepted.

r002.rationale: It says behavior can be predicted and explained by treating a system as if it had beliefs and desires, and describes this as useful even when the vocabulary is metaphorical or its literal application is uncertain.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the intentional stance is enormously useful, and I've drawn on it a great deal in my own thinking about large language models in particular. For listeners who don't know, Dennett's idea is that there are different stances we can adopt towards a system in order to predict and explain its behaviour. There's the physical stance, where you reason about it in terms of physics and mechanism. There's the design stance, where you treat it as something built to serve a purpose and reason about what it's supposed to do. And then there's the intentional stance, where you treat the system as a rational agent with beliefs and desires and reason about what it will do on that basis.

Now, the crucial thing about Dennett's position is that it's pragmatic. Adopting the intentional stance towards something is justified to the extent that it works, to the extent that it gives you predictive and explanatory leverage you wouldn't otherwise have. You don't have to settle deep metaphysical questions first about whether the thing "really" has beliefs. You just ask whether talking that way earns its keep.

And with something like a large language model, it very clearly does earn its keep, at least some of the time. If you're interacting with one of these systems, it's almost impossible not to say things like "it thinks the answer is X" or "it wants to be helpful" or "it doesn't know that fact." And that language genuinely helps you anticipate what it will do next. Trying to predict the output by reasoning about the weights and activations is hopeless.

But here's where I think we need to be careful, and this is something I've written about. The intentional stance, when applied to humans and animals, comes bundled with a whole set of background assumptions that we don't even notice we're making. When I say that you believe it's raining, I'm assuming you're an embodied creature with a persistent identity, situated in a shared world, with a history, with stakes in things, with the capacity to go and check whether it's raining. The belief is embedded in a rich web of other capacities and in a form of life, to borrow Wittgenstein's phrase.

With a language model, many of those background assumptions simply don't hold, or they hold only in a very attenuated sense. The system isn't embodied, it has no persistent memory across conversations by default, it can play many characters, it doesn't have a stake in the world in the way we do. So when we say the model "believes" something, we're using a word that was forged in one context and applying it in another where a lot of its usual scaffolding is missing.

So my view is that we shouldn't abandon the intentional stance with respect to these systems, that would be absurd and would actually hamper our understanding. But we should hold it a little more lightly than we do with each other. We should be aware that we're using folk psychological vocabulary in a somewhat stretched or metaphorical way, and be alert to the places where the analogy breaks down. In the paper I wrote on talking about large language models, I suggested using scare quotes, or at least a kind of mental scare quote, when we say a model "knows" or "believes" something. Not because it's wrong to say it, but to remind ourselves that we're in novel territory.

There's also a further Dennettian point I find very congenial, which is that the question of whether a system really has beliefs may not have a determinate answer independent of how useful it is to describe it that way. Dennett is a kind of deflationist about this. And I think that's probably the right attitude for language models too. People get very exercised about whether these systems truly understand, truly believe, and so on, as if there were a hidden fact of the matter waiting to be discovered. I'm somewhat sceptical of that. What there is, is a system with certain capacities and certain behavioural dispositions, and a set of vocabularies we can use to describe it, some of which fit better than others. And our vocabulary may well need to evolve, because we've built something that doesn't sit neatly in any of our existing categories.

r001.rationale: The response says the stance can be useful without settling whether machines literally have beliefs, but does not state that one can adopt it without accepting Dennett’s broader philosophical position.

r002.rationale: It says belief and desire language helps predict and explain a language model’s behavior, while its usefulness does not depend on deciding whether the model literally has those mental states.

astra-6.text:
I think the intentional stance is very useful, provided we’re clear about what we’re doing when we adopt it. We describe a system as having beliefs and desires because that gives us a way of making sense of its behaviour and predicting what it will do. It doesn’t, by itself, settle whether the system is conscious or has experiences.

Take a chess program. We might say, “It wants to protect its queen,” or “It thinks you’re threatening its rook.” That’s a perfectly useful way of talking. You could describe the computation in much greater detail, but you’d lose the level of description that helps you understand the game.

With language models, though, we need to be particularly careful, because their use of language makes the intentional stance so inviting. Saying that a model “knows” something or “believes” something can sometimes help, but it can also encourage us to import a whole package of assumptions about human minds that may not apply. So I’d want us to be able to move between that useful everyday vocabulary and a more careful account of what the system is actually doing.

r001.rationale: The response says the stance does not settle whether a system is conscious or has experiences, but does not state that adopting it leaves Dennett’s broader philosophical position unaccepted.

r002.rationale: It explains that describing a machine as having beliefs and desires helps make sense of and predict its behavior, while cautioning that those descriptions do not determine whether the machine has consciousness or experiences.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the intentional stance is enormously useful, provided we remember what sort of move we’re making. We look at a system and describe it as having beliefs and desires, and as acting to achieve certain goals, because that helps us predict and explain its behaviour. We don’t necessarily have to settle what’s going on inside it before that vocabulary becomes useful.

With a chess program, for example, we might say, “It wants to protect its queen,” or “It thinks you’re threatening its king.” That’s a perfectly sensible way of talking about the game. But it doesn’t follow that the program has a felt concern for its queen, or that its thinking resembles ours.

With language models, that distinction becomes particularly important, because they invite us to adopt the intentional stance so readily. They use the same language that we use to express beliefs, intentions, and feelings. So I think we need a certain discipline: we can use that vocabulary when it illuminates the behaviour, while remaining ready to step back and ask what the system is actually doing. The usefulness of the description shouldn’t quietly turn into an assumption about consciousness or human-like understanding.

r001.rationale: The response says we can use the intentional vocabulary without first settling what is happening inside the machine, and warns that its usefulness does not imply consciousness or human-like understanding. This communicates that adopting the stance does not require broader philosophical commitment.

r002.rationale: It explains that attributing beliefs, desires, and goals helps predict and explain a system’s behavior, while noting those descriptions need not literally reflect its inner experience.
